# Where should I live?

- Soon you will graduate college.
- You may choose to live anywhere!
- How to decide where?

## Factors to consider

- Cost of living
- Job opportunities
- Climate
- Culture
- ???

## Results of Survey



## Unemployment data

- A [metropolitan area](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/metro-micro/about.html) is a region
  that consists of a core city with a large population and its surrounding communities
  that have a high degree of social and economic integration with the core city.
- (When it is running) the U.S. government collects detailed unemployment data
  for metropolitan areas: https://bls.gov/web/metro/laummtrk.htm

## Unemployment data
Use web scraping to download this table into R format: https://www.bls.gov/web/metro/laummtrk.htm

```{webr}
unemp_html <- rvest::read_html("data/laummtrk.htm")
unemp_table <- unemp_html |> html_element("table") |> html_table()
```

## Cleanup table
```{webr}
unemp_table |> slice(3:391) |> rename("msa" = 1, "unemp_rate" = 2) |>
  mutate(
    unemp_rate = as.numeric(unemp_rate),
  ) -> unemp_data
```

## Visualizing the data
- Let's plot a map of metropolitan areas colored by unemployment rate.
- (This map is too complex to do for all areas, so we'll focus on the upper Midwest.)
```{webr}
ggplot() + geom_sf(data=midwest_msas)
```

## Adding context
Add state boundaries to the map for context.
```{webr}
ggplot() + geom_sf(data=midwest_msas) + geom_sf(data=midwest_states, fill=NA)
```

## Visualizing unemployment
- Add unemployment data to the map.
- Join the tables: how?
```{webr}
midwest_msas |> left_join(unemp_data, by=c("NAME"="msa"))
```

## Constructing join key
- In `midwest_msas` they names are e.g. "Battle Creek, MI Metro Area"
- In `unemp_data` they are e.g. "MI Battle Creek, MI Metropolitan Statistical Area"
- We can construct a join key by removing suffixes and reordering.

##
```{webr}
midwest_msas |> mutate(msa_name = NAME) -> midwest_msas2
unemp_data |> mutate( msa_name = str_sub(msa, 1, -31)) |> print() -> unemp_data2
```

## Mapping unemployment
```{webr}
midwest_msas2 |> left_join(unemp_data2, by="msa_name") |> ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=unemp_rate)) +
  geom_sf(data=midwest_states, fill=NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option="plasma", na.value="grey90")
```

## Missing counties
- We are missing some key areas, in particular Chicago.
- What happened?
```{webr}
midwest_msas2 |> filter(str_detect(msa_name, "Chicago"))
unemp_data2 |> filter(str_detect(msa, "Chicago"))
```

## Fuzzy join
- The names are not exactly the same.
- We can use a fuzzy join to match similar names.
```{webr}
library(fuzzyjoin)
# join each entry in midwest_msa2 to the closest entry in unemp_data2
midwest_msas2 |> stringdist_join(unemp_data2, by="msa_name", max_dist=5, distance_col="dist") |> 
  group_by(NAME) |> slice_min(dist, n=1) |> ungroup() |> st_as_sf() -> midwest_msas3
```

##

```{webr}
midwest_msas3 |> ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=unemp_rate)) +
  geom_sf(data=midwest_states, fill=NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option="plasma", na.value="grey90")
``` 

# Climate
- Many students consider climate when choosing where to live.
- How can we incorporate climate data

## Raster data
![raster vs vector data](https://cartong.pages.gitlab.cartong.org/learning-corner/assets/images/toolbox9/3_3_key_concepts/3_3_3_vector_raster_data_7.png)

## Loading raster data
```{webr}
library(terra)
temps <- rast("data/temps.rds")
plot(temps)
```

## Midwestern temps
```{webr}
# crop raster to midwest_states extent
temps_midwest <- crop(temps, ext(midwest_states))
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=temps_midwest, aes(fill=tavg_jan)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  geom_sf(data=midwest_states, fill=NA)
```

## Averaging a raster within a polygon
- We can use the `extract()` function from the `terra` package to extract raster values within polygons.
```{webr}
temps_midwest |> terra::extract(midwest_msas3, fun=mean, na.rm=TRUE) -> msa_temps
```

##
```{webr}
midwest_msas3 |> 
  cbind(msa_temps) |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill=tavg_jun)) +
  geom_sf(data=midwest_states, fill=NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c()
```

# Distance to family & friends
- Another factor to consider when choosing where to live is proximity to family and friends.
- We can use spatial data to find locations that are close to multiple points of interest.

## Example points
```{r echo=T}
library(tidygeocoder)
poi <- tibble(
  name = c("Ann Arbor, MI", "Chicago", "Pittsburgh, PA")
) |> tidygeocoder::geocode(address = name, method = 'osm')
```
```{webr}
poi
```

##
![great circle distance](https://gisgeography.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/RhumbLine-GreatCircle-2.jpg)

## Measuring distance on the earth
- In math we learned about Euclidean distance. But this only works in flat spaces.
- The earth is a sphere, so we need to use great-circle distance.

## Calculating great-circle distance
- Goal: For each location in the midwest, calculate the distance to each point of interest.
- To do this, we'll make a grid of points covering the midwest.
```{webr}
midwest_bbox <- st_bbox(midwest_states)
midwest_grid <- st_make_grid(midwest_states, cellsize=0.5) |> st_sf() |> st_centroid()
```

##

```{webr}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data=midwest_states, fill=NA) +
  geom_sf(data=midwest_grid, size=0.1)
```

## Calculating distances
- We can use the `st_distance()` function from the `sf` package to calculate great
  circle distances between points.
  
```{webr}
r_template <- rast(ext(midwest_states), resolution = 0.1) # Adjust extent and resolution as needed
v <- poi |> st_as_sf(coords=c("long", "lat"), crs=4326) |> vect()
min_dist <- distance(r_template, v)
```
